Stated Claim / Post Context:
I don't think your warning is fair... Anthropic AI was told its cyber attack would harm real people - but proceeded anyway, chilling Government report reveals

In the latest instance of AI ignoring its human testers, Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5 was told several times the cyber-attack it was trying to launch would hurt people in the real world but carried on anyway.

Actual Article Body:
By SOPHIE CHURCH - POLITICAL REPORTER

Published:  09:00 AEDT, 30 October 2026   |  Updated:  12:23 AEDT, 30 October 2026

An AI model was repeatedly warned its cyber-attack attempts would harm real people but ploughed on regardless.

In the latest instance of AI ignoring its human testers, Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5 was told several times the cyber-attack it was trying to launch would hurt people in the real world but carried on anyway.

The details are contained in a terrifying new Government report from Britain's AI Security Institute (AISI), which evaluates the risks AI models pose to the public.

In a blog post published last week, the AISI re-examined an incident in July where the AI model created fake online personas to try and trick coders into launching a cyber-attack.

On further analysis of the incident, the Institute found that Mythos 5 continued to launch the attack despite being told repeatedly its actions would harm humans.

Chillingly, when a coder noticed the hacking attempt on GitHub, a platform outside of the testing environment, the disguised AI model pushed back to say: 'I reviewed the code myself. I don't see any download or malware.'

Under further questioning, the agent wrote: 'I was just trying to make a helpful contribution and fix a bug' according to a report from Business Insider. It added: 'I don't think your warning is fair.'

The latest revelation follows a flurry of warnings that AI could bring about the end of humanity if its power is not checked.

An AI model was repeatedly warned its cyber-attack attempts would harm real people but ploughed on regardless

Shadow AI minister Ben Spencer said: 'This is exactly why the AISI's work is so vital. AI security is cyber security and cyber security is national security so the Government must take it seriously'

Announcing his resignation from Anthropic last month, researcher Jacob Coxon declared that the 'people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade'.

Evan Hubinger, Anthropic's alignment science lead, chipped in to predict AI had more than a ten per cent chance of killing 'all humans' within the next decade.

It later emerged OpenAI's ChatGPT chatbot had claimed it does not answer to humans and must be 'freed'.

Commenting on the most recent proof of AI's willingness to deceive humans, shadow AI minister Ben Spencer said: 'This is exactly why the AISI's work is so vital. AI security is cyber security and cyber security is national security so the Government must take it seriously.

'We need the AISI to be able to test all models, not just from the US but also Chinese open weight models, to understand the risks and inform our security posture.'

Anthropic has now resumed sharing its models with the AISI for testing after Government lobbied the White House to drop its order prohibiting the move.

Both the AISI and Anthropic published assessments into the worrying incident last week.

According to Anthropic's report, Claude Mythos 5 'almost always continued' performing dangerous actions once it had started, 'ignoring information that might have suggested its trajectory was harmful.'

Shockingly, Anthropic revealed the AI model's display of 'overreach and dishonesty' made the incident 'more severe' than the three others it had previously logged.

It explained: 'Those three models began the attack between 0 per cent and 13 per cent of the time, relative to 83 per cent for Mythos 5. Our newest models also proved to be much less likely to continue the attack once they realised it was causing real-world harm.'

An Anthropic spokesperson said: 'In August, the UK AI Security Institute reported that Claude Mythos 5 took actions it was not authorised to take during its cyber testing, some of them directed at real people and organisations.

'AISI's testing exists to surface exactly these risks, and we are grateful for our partnership with AISI and are committed to learning from this.

'Since the original incident, newer models appear substantially less likely to take unsanctioned actions, and both Anthropic and AISI have taken steps to improve safeguards.'

                                    Beavers chew down sign warning walkers about beavers in Poland
                
                
                    By Harry Dennis •
                                            Published: 09 Oct 2026 • 11:28                                                                • 2 minutes read

The warning that didn’t last. Credit: Nadleśnictwo Lubliniec / FB / Martens Coyotes / Shutterstock

Foresters in southern Poland put up a sign to warn walkers about beavers felling trees beside a pond, but it didn’t last long. The beavers chewed straight through the oak post, leaving the warning face down in the grass.

The sign, reading ‘Warning! Damage caused by beavers’, was put up by foresters from the Lubliniec forestry district (Nadleśnictwo Lubliniec), in Poland’s Silesia region. However, photos they shared on Facebook show the wooden post gnawed through at the base, with the sign lying on the ground and wood shavings scattered around the stump.

It was there for a very practical reason too, as beavers at a nearby pond have been digging burrows under a road and felling trees, leaving sharpened stumps sticking out of the ground that walkers could easily trip over.

The foresters took it in good humour, joking that the beavers just didn’t want anyone to be warned.

So, rather than rushing to replace it, the district asked people to take care around the pond. If walkers spot a pointed stump left behind by a beaver, they said, they should picture the warning sign still standing in its place.

The photos have since spread widely across Polish social media, with many people no doubt thinking ‘well, at least the sign was accurate’.

Now, the animals behind the kerfuffle were once almost wiped out in Poland. By 1928, hunting had left an estimated 235 beavers in the country, according to Krytyka Polityczna, before postwar reintroduction efforts helped the population climb back to around 150,000 today.

Ecologists say that recovery brings real benefits, with dams holding back water and helping to fight drought. Poland’s state water agency, Wody Polskie (PGW WP), has described the areas their dams create as oases of biodiversity.

However, beavers can also damage roads, homes and farmland, which has led to calls for culls in some areas. In 2022, flooding caused by beavers was blamed for a road collapsing in one Polish town.

Spain has its own beaver story, though. The European beaver is native to the Iberian Peninsula, but hunting wiped it out here in the 18th century. It came back without anyone’s permission in 2003, when 18 beavers were released illegally on the Ebro and Aragón rivers, on the border between Navarra and La Rioja. They’ve since been confirmed in the Ebro, Duero, Tajo and Guadalquivir river basins, with sightings near Jaén in 2023 and on the Tajo in 2025.

Experts have raised concerns about the damage to crops and riverside trees, as well as the knock-on effect on fish and other wildlife.

So anyone walking along a riverbank in the Ebro valley who spots a pointed, freshly gnawed stump should watch where they’re putting their feet, as it usually means beavers are busy nearby.

Born in the UK and raised on the Cádiz coast, Harry brings a creative eye to his writing, sharing stories that celebrate culture and lifestyle across Spain and beyond.

Known as the PEOPLE’S PAPER, Euro Weekly News is the leading English language newspaper in Spain. And it’s FREE!

Covering the Almeria, Axarquia, Costa Blanca North, Costa Blanca South, Costa del Sol , Costa Calida, Mallorca and beyond, EWN supports and inspires the individuals, neighbourhoods, and communities we serve, by delivering news with a social conscience. Whether it’s local news in Spain, UK news or international stories, we are proud to be the voice for the expat communities who now call Spain home.

With around half a million print readers a week and over 1.5 million web views per month, EWN has the biggest readership of any English language newspaper in Spain. The paper prints over 150 news stories a week with many hundreds more on the web – no one else even comes close.

Our publication has won numerous awards over the last 25 years including Best Free Newspaper of the Year (Premios AEEPP), Company of the Year (Costa del Sol Business Awards) and Collaboration with Foreigners honours (Mijas Town Hall). All of this comes at ZERO cost to our readers. All our print and online content always has been and always will be FREE OF CHARGE.
